newsitem.title: USA: Du Pont was insane when he killed wrestler-lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Du Pont was insane when he killed wrestler-lawyer.

text.p: Millionaire chemicals heir John du Pont acted from within an "abyss of insanity" when he killed Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz, du Pont's lawyer told a jury Monday.

In opening statements in du Pont's murder trial, attorney Thomas Bergstrom said du Pont, 58, had suffered from paranoid schizophrenia for years and the disease reached a new intensity on Jan. 26, 1996, when he shot Schultz.
"What happened that day is simply not in dispute," Bergstrom said. "John du Pont shot David Schultz, backed his car out of the driveway and went home.

"This case is about a killing for no reason whatsoever at the hand of a man who suffered from a mental disease which took away his ability to know what he was doing was wrong," Bergstrom said, outlining the insanity defence du Pont's lawyers will use in the case.

Referring to du Pont's approach to the Schultz home at the far end of du Pont's Foxcatcher estate, Bergstrom said, "John du Pont drove his Lincoln Town Car out of the front gate of his estate and into the abyss of insanity."

Du Pont is being tried on charges of first degree murder in the killing of Schultz, a coach at a wrestling training facility du Pont had established on the estate. If convicted on the first-degree charge he faces life in prison.
Lead prosecutor Joseph McGettigan said in his opening statement du Pont killed Schultz for the common criminal reasons of "jealousy, envy, revenge, (and) anger."

"He knew what he did and he knew that it was wrong," McGettigan said. In his statement, he gave new details of the prosecution's version of the killing, including what he said were Schultz's last words.

As Schutlz's widow, Nancy, looked on in the courtroom, McGettigan said Schultz emerged from a car he was working on when du Pont and a security consultant drove up. Schultz then greeted du Pont with the words "Hi, coach."
Du Pont then raised his arm from inside the car, a .44 magnum revolver in his hand, and said, "Do you have a problem with me?" and fired the first of three shots into Schultz before driving away.

Bergstrom said du Pont had been driven by delusions and paranoia. Those delusions often centred around Schultz and du Pont's paranoia often went "right through the roof" in the presence of his security consultants.

He said du Pont believed people lived in his walls and that "mechanical trees" on his estate took things from him. Du Pont also believed himself to be the Dalai Lama, the Christ Child, and the last czar of Russia.
Bergstrom cited Nancy Schultz' own words in support of his case, saying when an emergency 911 operator asked why du Pont would kill her husband she replied, "He's insane."

Both sides in the case said tapes of conversations held with du Pont during a 48-hour standoff with police after the killings would provide key support for their positions. In the tapes, du Pont asked for his lawyers and gave other signs he was aware of the position he was in, McGettigan said. But Bergstrom said he also reiterated his delusional claims.

Du Pont had been brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair, the result of a knee injury Friday while being taken back to the hospital where is being confined. He wore a blue sweatsuit of his Foxcatcher wrestling team and his drawn face was framed by shaggy gray hair and beard. He watched the court session with heavy lidded eyes and said little.
Nancy Schultz was expected to be the first witness when court resumed after an afternoon break Monday.
